READING

**Mapping the requirements**

The Local Voice tier has three tests at the February 2028 — sorry, February 2027 — snapshot: (a) fourteen hours a week of originated speech, (b) commissioned production no more than half of that originated total, and (c) thirty registered contributors. I will work through each course against all three, then look at the financial and structural tail.

---

**Course ELSWICK against the three tests**

*Hours.* Nine in-house plus six commissioned equals fifteen hours a week. Against the fourteen-hour floor, that is one hour clear — not a squeaker. Contract start is 2026-10-05, well before the four-week measurement window, so Halverston is fully embedded in the schedule by the time the clocks start.

*Commissioned proportion.* Six hours commissioned out of fifteen total originated is 40 %. The cap is 50 %. ELSWICK clears this by ten percentage points.

*Contributors.* The count stands at 34. Commissioned producers do not join the register, so no change from ELSWICK itself. I need to check whether organic decline will erode the buffer. From 41 in 2024 to 34 now is a loss of seven over roughly twenty months, a net run-rate of about 4.2 a year or 0.35 a month. From August 2026 to the February 2027 snapshot is six months. Projected further loss: roughly two contributors. Projected count at snapshot: approximately 32. That is two above the 30-contributor floor. Not a wide cushion, but a real one.

ELSWICK clears all three tests at the first opportunity with high confidence.

---

**Course CRANMOOR against the three tests**

*Hours.* This is where CRANMOOR carries serious execution risk. The station needs to grow from nine to fourteen hours of originated speech. The brief says that requires approximately fifteen additional active contributing volunteers. In the whole of 2025, without a coordinator, the station added nine contributors across twelve months. Even with a coordinator from 2026-10-01, the February window closes in five months. To reach fifteen net new active producers in five months, the station would need to run at roughly three times its 2025 recruitment pace — and new volunteers typically need onboarding time before they are reliably producing content that can be scheduled. A realistic scenario under CRANMOOR at February 2027 is perhaps five to ten genuinely active new voices, adding one to two hours a week, bringing the total to ten to eleven hours, still two to four hours short of the threshold.

*Commissioned proportion.* Under CRANMOOR, commissioned hours are zero, so the cap is not a concern either way.

*Contributors.* The coordinator works the register as well as the schedule, so attrition is more likely to be arrested or reversed. The contributor count at February 2027 would probably hold at 33-34 or improve slightly. CRANMOOR very likely passes the contributor test even if it fails the hours test.

CRANMOOR probably passes two of three tests in February 2027 but misses the hours threshold.

---

**The cost of a missed February**

The problem statement is explicit: a station short in February is reassessed on 2027-08-31, with payment starting the month it clears. The four-year term runs from 2027-04-01 either way. This means missing February is not merely a deferral — it is a permanent forfeiture of the grant income from April through to the month before clearing.

If CRANMOOR misses February and clears August, payment begins September 2027. That is five months without grant income (April through August). Against £96,000 a year, five months represents £40,000 of grant receipts permanently gone; the four-year term does not extend to compensate. The reserve of £62,000 would cover the cash shortfall from fixed costs in that window (roughly £24,000), and the coordinator salary during the gap adds another £8,750, so solvency is not in doubt — but £40,000 of income that will never arrive is a material loss on a £96,000-a-year grant.

If CRANMOOR fails August as well, the loss compounds further and the reserve position becomes stressed.

---

**Annual cost comparison**

ELSWICK: £20,280 a year (6 hours × £65 × 52 weeks).
CRANMOOR: £21,000 a year in salary and on-costs.

These are effectively identical recurring outlays, both inside the board's £22,000 cap. Neither course has a meaningful cost advantage in year-one terms.

---

**Longer-term structural picture**

CRANMOOR does have real advantages that ELSWICK does not: the hours produced are owned and do not need to be repurchased, and the coordinator addresses the declining contributor trend that ELSWICK leaves entirely unattended. If the register continues to drift toward 30 under ELSWICK, there is a risk of failing the contributor test at some future Local Voice compliance check within the four-year period.

However, once the Local Voice grant is in payment — which ELSWICK secures by April 2027 — the board's constraint on new recurring commitments lifts. At that point the station could explore adding a part-time coordinator alongside or in lieu of Halverston (the Halverston contract rolls on twelve-month terms, so it can be exited). ELSWICK does not foreclose CRANMOOR-style capacity building; it sequences it to a moment of greater financial stability. CRANMOOR attempted before the grant is confirmed risks the entire funding position for a structural benefit that is, in any case, achievable eighteen months later.

---

**Summary of the deciding logic**

ELSWICK delivers fifteen hours, 40 % commissioned, and approximately 32 contributors at the February 2027 snapshot — clearing all three Local Voice tests in one pass. CRANMOOR almost certainly does not reach fourteen hours by February 2027 given the pace of volunteer recruitment and activation against a five-month runway, which means it likely triggers the reassessment mechanism and permanently forfeits up to £40,000 in grant income. Both options cost about £20,500-£21,000 a year. The certainty of clearing in February under ELSWICK decisively outweighs CRANMOOR's long-term structural attractions, which remain available to pursue once the grant is secured.

---

CALL
  ELSWICK

GROUNDS
  CRANMOOR cannot realistically recruit and activate the fifteen additional contributing volunteers needed to reach fourteen hours within the five-month window before the February 2027 assessment, making a missed first test — and the permanent forfeiture of up to £40,000 in grant income — the most probable outcome, whereas ELSWICK clears all three Local Voice criteria at the first attempt with near-certainty at effectively the same annual cost.
